lead: Software maintenance is the work done on a system after delivery to keep it useful. It exists because a live system faces new platforms, new rules, defects and user needs. Re-engineering is the larger step: when patching an old system costs too much, engineers recover its design, improve its structure and rebuild it. Maintenance and re-engineering are used in payroll, banking, ticketing and government systems that must keep running while they change.
prereq: You need: the software life cycle from Unit 1, quality assurance from 6.7, and configuration control from 6.6.

blocks.text: Maintenance is not only bug fixing. Textbooks divide it into four types by why the change is made. Maintenance cost is the effort and money spent on changes after delivery.

items: Corrective maintenance fixes defects found after delivery. Example: a UPI payment fails when the amount has two decimal places.
Adaptive maintenance changes the system for a new environment or rule. Example: move to a new database, or support a new tax rule.
Perfective maintenance improves what the user can see or feel, such as speed, usability or a new report. It changes the product even when no defect exists.
Preventive maintenance improves future work. Example: rewrite a confusing module before it causes defects, or add tests to a fragile area.

blocks.text: The same change can look like two types. A new tax rule is adaptive; a faster screen is perfective. The label matters because managers budget and plan each type differently. For long-lived systems, maintenance can be the largest part of total cost. Each change needs analysis, code, test and release. Units are hours or rupees.

A change request starts the maintenance process. The team records the request, classifies it, and estimates the work. Next comes impact analysis: find every module, database field, interface and test that the change can affect. A small code edit can break a report, a batch job or another team's API.

items: Record the change request and classify its maintenance type.
Find affected modules, data, interfaces and tests.
Implement the change on a branch.
Run regression tests and review the result.
Release the change and update records.

blocks.text: Impact analysis uses traceability links from requirements to design to code and tests. Configuration management from 6.6 supplies versions and baselines. After the change, regression testing from Unit 4 checks old behaviour. Release management from 6.9 moves the change to production.
S = (R<sub>old</sub> − R<sub>new</sub>) × H; P = C ÷ S
blocks.where: S is yearly saving in hours; R<sub>old</sub> is old change requests per year; R<sub>new</sub> is new count after re-engineering; H is hours per request; P is payback in years; C is re-engineering effort in hours.

blocks.text: The payback P is used later when deciding whether to re-engineer.

A legacy system is an old system that still runs important work but is hard to change. It may have missing documentation, old languages, tight coupling and no tests. It is risky to discard because business rules live only in its code.

Options are: keep patching, re-engineer, replace, or retire. Re-engineering has three technical steps: reverse engineering (recover design), restructuring (improve structure without changing behaviour) and rebuilding on the new platform. Reverse engineering reads code and recovers modules, data, interfaces and rules. Restructuring, also called refactoring, improves internal structure without changing behaviour. Rebuilding changes the system to a new form: new language, new platform, new database or new architecture.

The figure adds the starting legacy system and the resulting new system, so it shows five boxes but only three re-engineering steps. Re-engineering is not always a big-bang rewrite. Teams often move one module at a time and keep the old system live until the new one is proven. This lowers risk but needs careful interfaces.

figure.caption: The path from old code to a new system: recover design, improve structure without changing behaviour, then rebuild on the new platform.

spec.title: Re-engineering path
spec.aria: Legacy code is reverse engineered, refactored and rebuilt into a new system.

examples.question: A payroll system gets 500 change requests a year; each costs 8 hours. Re-engineering costs 3,000 hours and is expected to cut requests to 100 a year. Compute yearly saving and payback in years and months.
steps: Old yearly effort = 500 × 8 = 4,000 hours per year.
New yearly effort = 100 × 8 = 800 hours per year.
Yearly saving S = 4,000 − 800 = 3,200 hours per year. Check: (500 − 100) × 8 = 3,200.
Payback P = re-engineering effort ÷ yearly saving = 3,000 ÷ 3,200 = 0.9375 years.
examples.answer: Yearly saving is 3,200 hours per year; payback is 0.9375 years, about 11.25 months.
examples.check:
old = 500
new = 100
hours = 8
cost = 3000
saving = (old - new) * hours
payback = cost / saving
months = payback * 12
print(float(saving))
print(float(payback))
print(float(months))

traps: Calling every change corrective maintenance. Maintenance also adapts to new platforms and improves future work.
Saying reverse engineering changes behaviour. It recovers design; restructuring changes structure without changing behaviour.
Using payback = saving ÷ cost. Correct payback = one-time cost ÷ yearly saving.
Treating preventive and perfective maintenance as the same. Preventive reduces future risk; perfective improves current user-visible quality.
Writing that maintenance ends at delivery. Maintenance starts after delivery and continues while the system is live.

quiz.a: Corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive maintenance.

quiz.q: Why is impact analysis needed before a maintenance change?
quiz.a: It finds the modules, data, interfaces and tests that the change can affect. It prevents hidden breakage and guides the estimate and regression plan.

quiz.q: A system gets 200 requests a year at 5 hours each. Re-engineering costs 1,500 hours and cuts requests to 50 a year. Find yearly saving and payback.
quiz.a: Old effort = 200 × 5 = 1,000 hours per year. New effort = 50 × 5 = 250 hours per year. Saving = 1,000 − 250 = 750 hours per year. Payback = 1,500 ÷ 750 = 2 years.

quiz.q: A team reverse engineers a legacy system but does not restructure it. What can go wrong?
quiz.a: The team learns the design but leaves poor structure in place. Future changes stay costly and risky, so the maintainability gain is small.
An old but business-critical system that is hard to change because of missing documentation, old technology or tight coupling.

quiz.q: A change touches 3 modules, but tests exist for only 1 module. What should impact analysis list?
quiz.a: It should list all 3 affected modules, their interfaces and data, plus 2 modules with missing tests. The plan must add tests and run regression on all 3.

quiz.q: What is the difference between restructuring and re-engineering?
quiz.a: Restructuring improves internal structure without changing behaviour. Re-engineering changes the system to a new form, such as a new platform, language or architecture.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, re-engineering often appears as technical-debt reduction, automated refactoring, static analysis and cloud migration. The strangler fig pattern moves traffic from a legacy system to new services one route at a time. Researchers study code smells, clone detection and program comprehension tools.
